speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with Bill C-26 which is legislation that would make legal the interception and opening of mail in two general areas. The first of these is the criminal area, in which the bill purports to assist in the battle against drug traffic. The second area relates to national security, wherein the bill purports to assist in the prevention or detection of subversive activities.
This second reading debate upon which we embark tonight is generally regarded as a debate in principle, and I think it is incumbent upon me at the outset of my remarks to make very clear the principle which we as the Official Opposition support. We support in principle the legal interception of mail in special specified circumstances, given adequate safeguards and given the situation where the more normal, acceptable and traditional methods of law enforcement have proven ineffective. Therefore, we support Bill C-26 in principle. In our view it meets most of these requirements. We do not anticipate a prolonged second reading debate, but I think contributions might be made from all corners of the House.
I agree with the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) that it is important this legislation reach its proper forum which, in my view, is the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
In enunciating the principle contained in the legislation i referred to the legal interception of mail. There is nothing much that is new about that. Indeed, I am informed that most countries in the western world have legislation of this nature. In England, for example, the legal interception of mail was recorded as long ago as 1663. In the same country we can find statutes permitting this interception that are over 200 years old, and those statutes relate to interception as a means of attacking serious crime and as a means for the preservation of the safety of the state.
In talking about the principle of the bill, I also referred to special and specified circumstances and to the necessary, proper safeguards. The interception of mail or of any form of communication is inherently objectionable-surely few of us will disagree with that-and it is objectionable for three reasons. The first is that the power to intercept is in the hands of the state and its officials and it is exercised secretly; the extent and the purpose of the use of the power is not publicly known. Second, the uncontrolled use of this power by the government might be an unnecessary interference with the private rights of a country's citizens. Third, the powers can be exercised without an opportunity for protest or objection. Therefore, the power to intercept a communication must never be a general power. It must be carefully restricted, it must be applicable to well defined circumstances, it must be the subject of special safeguards.
March 14, 1978

It is almost trite for me to say that this legislation infringes on the basic freedom of the individual, but there is a corollary: that freedom is of precious little value if the individual is the victim of the law breaker or the subversive. Indeed, in terms of national security, when that is under attack and no adequate defence is available, that basic freedom has the potential of becoming meaningless by its elimination.
However, on balance what I really seek is the assurance that there will be strict observance of the purposes to which the interception of mail should be directed or confined, and I look to the government, through its Solicitor General, for that assurance. I do not look to the law enforcement agencies of this country. I do not look to the security service officials. I look to the Solicitor General and the government that he represents to assure me that proper safeguards are in place and are working. I look to him to assure me that the power is restricted and used appropriately; and I look to the Solicitor General to assure me that the power is not to be used as a matter of routine and as simply a substitute for the conventional law enforcement measures that are our tradition.
Acknowledging that the reality of our times is that crime and subversive activity do occur in Canada, and further acknowledging that our law enforcement and security services must contend with these threats, we look to the Solicitor General and the government for a final assurance. Can they assure us that it is necessary to compromise further the fundamental right of privacy in order to protect us effectively from the threats of crime and subversion?
There is no doubt that the Solicitor General and the government would give these assurances that I seek. The question is not whether they will give them but rather how valid are they once given. Because this is a government which gives assurances at any time, in any place, about anything. We have had assurances in the House that there were no illegal or irregular security service activities. How quickly that proved wrong! We have had assurances in the House that these incidents amounted to one or two in number and were isolated. How quickly that proved wrong! We have had assurances that the McDonald Royal Commission was going to solve all these problems, but once the commission was constituted events alone overtook it and left it far behind. We have had assurances that no members of parliament were subjected to electronic surveillance. There are many in the House and in this country that doubt that assurance. Most recently we have had an assurance about the extreme sensitivity of a particular top secret document, and yet there are widely circulated reports, which are uncontradicted, that some 58 copies of that so-called top secret, sensitive document have been distributed around this capital.
Let us be more relevant. Let us talk about assurances on mail opening, which is the subject matter of this bill. In July 1975, in the House, the then solicitor general, now Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), assured us that first class mail cannot be opened. The then postmaster general, Bryce Mackasey, in 1975 gave the same assurance in the House.
Criminal Code
The present Solicitor General in his former role as postmaster general said the same thing in the House of Commons last November, only to be contradicted moments later by the then solicitor general, who got his news from the CBC. On November 9 the present Solicitor General told the House that he had checked with the Post Office's security and investigation officers. He assured us that there was no problem, but the director of the security intelligence branch of that department told the McDonald Commission that he knew about these instances in or about mid-October.
Why have all the assurances proved to be so false and so hollow? If one were a cynic, one would have to say that the motive for giving that type of assurance was simply to protect the political skin of he and they who gave it. That would be if one were cynical. If one were generous, one would say that these assurances which have been so false and so hollow were given to allay the suspicion and cynicism of Canadians. However, the result has been just exactly the opposite.
The bumbling, stumbling, fumbling and heavy-handed ineptitude of this government has been the very food for the cancer which has caused the suspicion and cynicism not just of members of this House but of Canadians everywhere. How did we get there? Where did this ineptitude come from? I think I know. It comes from the extraordinary and remarkable doctrine of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding ministerial responsibility. I am not sure 1 can put it as succinctly as he can, but I can paraphrase. The Prime Minister gathers his cabinet around him and gives them the following marching orders: "For heaven's sake, do not inform yourself about what is going on in your department. Above all, do not ask the right questions of your departmental officials. Cloud yourself and shroud yourself in ignorance, because as long as you can survive without a criminal charge being brought against you, we will all be all right". That is the doctrine, and that is the feed and the fodder for the cynicism and suspicion which is abounding in this country.
In this atmosphere along comes Bill C-26, to permit the legal interception of mail. The Solicitor General knows full well that the reaction is cynicism and suspicion. There has been a virtual litany of editorial comments, and I will quickly quote a few. "It," meaning this legislation, "is at best premature. It is also opportunistic, threatening and profoundly distressing". Another editorial: "To legalize the opening of mail is an act of contempt remarkable even by the generous standard of Pierre Trudeau". Another one: "A piece of tough anti-crime legislation that will be popular at election time". Another one: "A rush to amend a law that has not been enforced". "Retroactive sanction of illegal activities". The editorials go on and on.
This is the atmosphere in which this House and a diligent, hard working Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs must deal with this extremely important legislation. Who is to blame? It is not the opposition or Canadians from coast to coast. Those who are to blame sit on the government benches opposite, those whose irresponsibility is remarkable

and third, we have the Mackenzie Royal Commission recommendation that is now nine years old.
In face of all this, what do we have? We have the then solicitor general in 1975, now the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), replying to questions put to him in this House about RCMP difficulties in dealing with narcotics traffickers because of the law prohibiting the opening of first class mail. On that day, July 23, 1975, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) put the following question:
Does the minister not feel there should be an amendment to the effect that, while the privacy of the mail should be protected, this kind of traffic should not in any way be condoned by the failure of parliament to act?
The then solicitor general replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that from to time the RCMP have indicated a concern over this. Sometimes they have felt that narcotics were being brought into the country in first class mail ... in those cases they have dealt with the matter by following the mail to its source. But they have not made a big issue of it and as far as I know they have not recommended that we change the first class mail system. However, I will check with the force to find out what their exact recommendations are.
How typical that is of the ineptitude and incompetence of the series of solicitors general we have had. It is a perfect example of the incompetence of this parade of solicitors general.
Let us move now to the principal actor in this farce, the right hon. Prime Minister, that great pursuer of subversives, that great defender of law and order, that great enemy of the criminal and the subversive whose diligence in these matters increases in direct proportion to the proximity of a general election. The curtain lifts with the Prime Minister at centre stage at his press conference on November 18, when he said: we had caught a Japanese red army terrorist by opening his mail. Not by intercepting it, Mr. Speaker. The then solicitor general was very careful never to mention in this House that they had opened any mail, but merely intercepted it. Despite what the solicitor general told us earlier this evening, the truth was that the RCMP had indeed uncovered this terrorist-and they are to be commended-because they used legal and effective police methods that are their heritage and their tradition. I say again, they should be commended for it.
Let no one doubt, however, despite what the solicitor general told us this evening, what the evidence before the McDonald Commission clearly was. It was not about the opening and examination of the content of any mail. As far as I know, the only content of mail was an application to the University of Toronto and that had nothing to do with the uncovering and deportation of the Red Army terrorist. Yet the Prime Minister at the press conference said:
But when you catch a terrorist because you have opened an envelope, I don't think the bulk of the Canadian people would think that even if it was technically a crime, it would be something that should bring the RCMP people to jail.
What nonsense. What a disservice to the RCMP. How misleading to the country are statements such as that. That was not his best line on the subject, Mr. Speaker, and it was not his best line on that day. Listen to this one. It was a big
Criminal Code
moment. Referring to the opening of mail the Prime Minister of this country said:
If they can catch a terrorist or hijacker or kidnapper once out of five, to me that is a pretty good average.
There are two things in that statement. First, you open the mail to catch terrorists, hijackers and kidnappers; and second, one out of five, or 20 per cent, is a pretty good conviction rate.
Let us go to the first point, the Prime Minister's position that mail should be opened to catch hijackers, terrorists or kidnappers, and let us relate that to this bill. Terrorists may be caught because the Official Secrets Act is now applicable to the Post Office Act. I agree with the Prime Minister. But he did not say anything about drugs or about trading in narcotics or heroin, which is the subject matter of this bill. In terms of criminal activity there is not one word in this bill about hijackers or kidnappers. This bill, according to the solicitor general, is, and I quote:
... the production or the emanation of a long process of analysis and a sequel to the privacy legislation.
It has absolutely nothing to do with hijackers' activities. The only criminal offence dealt with, and indeed it is a very serious one, is drug trafficking. The privacy legislation deals with all kinds of serious offences-intimidation, forgery, hijacking, kidnapping, extortion, fraud on the public, use of the mails to defraud, fraudulent stock exchange transactions, murder. This is the production or emanation of a long process of analysis? Garbage.
What about letter bombs, Mr. Speaker? If a letter bomb was directed to a zealous Crown attorney in an attempt to assassinate him, there is nothing in this legislation to protect him. What about hardcore pornography which has been the subject matter of weeks and hours of study in this parliament by a very diligent committee? There is not one word about pornography. This is the emanation of a long process of analysis? The only criminal activity dealt with is drug trafficking. I agree with it.
The Solicitor General tonight talked about crimes attributed to the use of heroin and other drugs, prostitution, murder and the increase of known addicts since 1965. My question to him is, what has he been doing about it? He has known about it since 1965. What has he been doing? Nothing. Hon. members should check the amendments to see how much legislation has dealt with the fight or the war against hard drugs. What cowards this government has been in that war.
The inclusion of the provisions to open mail legally in an attempt to fight drug trafficking was probably a last minute idea of someone to give some popular appeal to this legislation. If I were cynical that is the only conclusion I could really draw. What is the distinction between those offences subject to legal interception by electronic means and those offences subject to legal interception by the opening of the mail?
Let me come to the Prime Minister's second point, Mr. Speaker. His target of 20 per cent, a one in five success rate, is not acceptable. It is not even high enough to be considered

March 14, 1978
Criminal Code
mediocre. With respect to activity against subversives, one does not look to arrest rates as a measurement of success. I acknowledge that. There is less stress on the need for convictions in anti-subversive activity. The concern is to safeguard the state and to keep it informed about the activities of those acting against its national security. There have been 65 openings of mail apparently since 1970. The only success trotted out by the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General is the Japanese Red Army terrorists. What a hollow example that has proved to be.
Let us look at the criminal side of things. Twenty per cent is ridiculously low in terms of an arrest rate. In a four-year period in the United Kingdom there was a 57 per cent arrest rate as a result of telephone taps alone. In terms of matters wherein there were major customs frauds, the interceptions resulted in an 80 per cent arrest rate. But to the Prime Minister one in five, a 20 per cent rate, is good. I ask the Solicitor General to consider most seriously, with respect to criminal activities that the government include a provision that there be a good reason, not a probability, to conclude that an interception of mail would result in an arrest.
Moving on to the security side of things, the Post Office Act is now subject to the provisions of the Official Secrets Act. Providing this legislation is successfully concluded, mail may be opened legally to prevent or to detect subversive activity. We support that. The Official Secrets Act is not being amended. We may not debate it. There is no opportunity to review its provisions or to discuss them. Many Canadians and many of my colleagues in this House are concerned about vagueness in the bill. Many think there should be a review. The Solicitor General laughs, sir. I do not think there is anything funny about the Official Secrets Act. I think it is a very serious matter. I dare say that the committee might think it is serious in spite of, not because of, the Solicitor General. But with this government everything is secret.
That act gives sole discretion to the Solicitor General and inevitably it will lead to suspicion. The mere fact that the Solicitor General is a politician may lead to suspicion. The report to parliament is one page long. There is no provision in the Official Secrets Act that mail opening is not to become a routine matter. Therefore, in addition to suggesting that there should be a review of the Official Secrets Act, my main concern is this. Given a situation where everything is up to the Solicitor General's discretion, who is watching the Solicitor General? No one that I know of in this House wants to become privy to genuinely secret material, but our experience with this unhappy parade of solicitors general is that they have never taken to inform themselves. Why, sir? Because of the Prime Minister's extraordinary doctrine of ministerial irresponsibility; and secondly, because no one was watching the solicitor general. He was accountable to no one and is accountable to no one under the Official Secrets Act.
There are a host of other questions to be asked and the proper forum is in the standing committee. One may ask why are telegrams and cables not dealt with? One might ask who are the Solicitor General's agents authorized to apply for mail

opening warrants? Are they the provincial attorneys general? Are they all police officers? What will the monitoring system be? Monthly, quarterly, yearly? There is no indication. How many people will have access to this confidential information? There is a factor here, sir. Those 58 reports floating around Ottawa were not seen by 58 people. One has to multiply 58 by a factor, the factor being the number of pairs of eyes that have had access to those documents. What will the access to this material be? Will there be specific reports of interception of the mail to and from lawyers, their families, their employees and associates? No provision is made for that. Why not separate warrants for each individual whose mail is to be opened? Is there to be a uniform and elaborate system for keeping records? These are questions that should be properly dealt with in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
In the last parliament, the twenty-ninth parliament, a similar matter, the Protection of Privacy Act, went to that committee. The resulting legislation was good legislation as a result of the evidence adduced before it and the diligence and integrity of the members who contributed to the hearings of that committee. One must hope this legislation will achieve the same result.
In conclusion, I repeat again that we support in principle the legal interception of mail in special and specified circumstances provided there are adequate safeguards and provided also that the usual and customary methods of law enforcement have proved ineffective. In supporting it, I say to the Solicitor General that he and the government he represents have sorely tested-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened most carefully to the remarks of my good friend from Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis). Without any doubt he is becoming the Cicero of the Conservative party.

Someone says that they have the Cicero and we have the sissies. We will see how they vote on the bill. Then we will know who has the Cicero and who the sissies.
March 14, 1978

If I had any doubt whatsoever, the eloquence of the honourable member for Perth-Wilmot convinced me with regard to the right course of action to take in connection with this legislation. I hope it has convinced a few people on the other side of the House, because I understand there are a number on the government side who not only have severe reservations but may very well vote against the legislation. The reasons advanced by the honourable member for Perth-Wilmot are excellent reasons, not for supporting this bill in principle, but for voting against this bill in principle and voting against it on second reading.
Any fair examination of the record to date-and we heard the record read to us eloquently by the hon. member I referred to-clearly shows that if there is a danger in the legislation, it is to advance any further discretion to the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais). That is exactly what this bill does.
I want to commence my remarks by reading an editorial from the Globe and Mail which sums up the position that responsible members of this House must take. It is their editorial of January 30, 1978. I quote:
The interception of private mail by the police is threatening, not because we ourselves may fear the opening of our own mail, but because it is threatening in principle. The police have as great a duty to obey the law as has any private citizen. The law binds all men. This principle can be circumvented-but it cannot be obscured-by the granting of special legal privileges to the police. Such privileges exist, but they have a tentative existence; they cannot be granted wholesale or be permitted to take root. A privilege granted one day can far too easily be perceived the next day as a duty.
That has been the history of all the legislation passed in this House since I have come here. I refer to the electronics legislation and what we now have before us, the mail legislation. We have heard the argument about the Red terrorists captured allegedly as a result of opening the mail. The popular little number of narcotics has been specifically placed in the bill to catch the public eye and public support. As a result of this, we know that this bill is the most politically inspired piece of legislation to come forward in this session of parliament.
This bill is not designed to catch narcotics traffickers, but to delude the public and get a few extra votes. It will not do that. We are not going to let the cynicism and dishonesty of this government, in particular the cynicism of the Solicitor General, obscure the real reasons for this bill and the effect it will have.
We are not purists. In proper circumstances and at appropriate times it is not wrong for the mail to be opened with regard to certain specific offences, but only under circumstances where permission is granted by judicial warrant, where the person is specified and the particular piece of mail is specified. However, what we have before us is a shotgun approach to the subject of mail opening.
Were it only those provisions which dealt with specific offences under the Code, such as narcotics and food and drug control, and included were the protections of civil liberties, the notification of the individual, the judicial warrant and the specificity which is absent in the bill, I could agree with the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot that the bill could merit
Criminal Code
support in principle. However, that is not what we have before us.
The smallest clause in the bill is the most dangerous. If you read the bill quickly, you might miss it. I refer to Section 43 of the Post Office Act, printed on page 17 of the bill. It reads:
Notwithstanding anything in any other Act or law, nothing is liable to demand, seizure or detention while in the course of post except under the authority of a warrant issued pursuant to section 16 of the Official Secrets Act-
If you kept reading, you might miss something. You have to look at the Official Secrets Act to understand what that really means. Under the section referred to the in the Official Secrets Act, the Solicitor General of Canada may issue a warrant authorizing the interception or seizure of any communication for the prevention or detection of subversive activity. The bill goes on to define subversive activity. This is important. Subclause (c) reads:
-activities directed toward accomplishing governmental change within Canada or elsewhere by force or violence or any criminal means:
I emphasize "or any criminal means". This legislation gives to the Solicitor General an unbridled discretion to issue a warrant in determining which group he considers to be subversive, and any group can be subversive if they are suspected of using any criminal means.
Let me give the Solicitor General some examples of groups which could now become subject to the opening of mail at the hon. gentleman's discretion-and I am sure he will use that discretion in the broadest way he can, to judge by his record to date. Take, for example, one group which appears to be unpopular at the moment, the Greenpeace organization. The government recently made it an offence for anyone to go on the ice within half a mile of the seal herd. To do so carries a penalty under the criminal law. It would probably be a popular thing for the minister in present circumstances to issue warrants permitting all the mail of Greenpeace to be opened. That is just one example. I could mention many other groups, native groups, anti-poverty groups and so on.
In order to protect freedom, Mr. Speaker, you have to protect unpopular groups from attack by governments, and this bill is clearly an attack on the capacity of such groups to function in a normal political way.

We have heard some interesting argument as to the amount of evidence which has been before the McDonald Commission and the Keable Inquiry. The Solicitor General had something quite interesting to say about that. When some bright press reporter suggested this bill was premature, he defended it by saying-and I am quoting from the Vancouver Sun of February 18, 1978:
Governments can't stop operating and can't stop taking executive decisions because commissions are sitting.
I put it to the Solicitor General that when opposition members asked questions about what was going on before those commissions, the government ceased to function. It ceased to answer questions. It did absolutely nothing except stonewall the opposition. But when people suggest the minister should wait and see what Mr. McDonald recommends, we get the answer that the government cannot cease operating. It is a cynical, blatant, dishonest grab for votes, that is what it is, and it is not going to catch a single drug trafficker.
Look at the record on drug trafficking. There are many things the government could have done. There are many things it could do. One of them would be to institute a decent compulsory treatment program for heroin addicts. Another would be to set up registration procedures along lines which have been so successful around the world. But what has been the response of the government? It is: Let's open their mail!

I would be happy to put my seat on the line on the basis that the Solicitor General confirm that he is able to cut 10 per cent of the addiction in British Columbia as a result of opening mail. I do not think he can reduce any of the addiction by opening mail. What a silly argument in justification of this bill. That is why the comments of the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot were so apropos when he noted that the section applied only to narcotics, to drug addiction and that other offences such as kidnapping, murder and conspiracy to murder, rape and certain other offences under the Code did not appeal to the Solicitor General. No, this sounded like the one which would catch the eye of the public, the one he could cash in on best at election time.
We have come a long way in this country from the tradition of the liberty of the subject, from the concept that in a free society there should be some right to privacy somewhere. It is pretty well established that our telephone communications are not likely to be private, and now the Solicitor General is moving into the area of the mails.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman really understands what he is doing. I say this to members of the government: if you keep this up, you will change the whole character of the country; you will change the traditions which people have for so long enjoyed in western society. This is a dangerous government, Mr. Speaker. It is a dangerous government and a desperate government which would take this particular measure as a quick vote-getting gimmick to try to perpetuate itself in office. I do not believe the people of Canada will fall for this legislation. I believe they will see it for what it is, phony from the word "Go". I hate to try to give lessons to an eminent lawyer like the Solicitor General on the subject of the rule of law-

speechtext:
-but those of us who have had a little training in the law ought, perhaps, to return to law school again to study that principle, that the rule of law is for you and for me and for the police and for everyone. But when the police violate the law, as they have done with regard to mail in a massive way, not a single charge is laid against them.
I am not suggesting those police officers should go to jail. What I am suggesting is that the law should apply to all of us equally. To react to a fairly massive violation of the privacy of the mail with a bill to legalize it gives us on this side a good understanding of where the sensibilities of the Solicitor General lie on the subject of the rule of law. The difficulty for the present Solicitor General, as for his two predecessors in office, lies in his inability to distinguish between the interest of the Liberal party and the interest of Canada. They think they are one and the same. They have been in office so long it has now become impossible for them to distinguish between those two things. But they are different. They are very different. We are again about to embark upon a serious erosion of the rights we have come to enjoy because of tough forebears, including those who went out in world war two and died on the beaches of Dieppe to maintain freedom in Canada. I am sick and tired of watching this government squander these rights and freedoms every time it thinks it can get a quick vote through a piece of legislation.
How many convictions have we seen as a result of the opening of mail, based on the evidence before the Keable or McDonald inquiries? I suggest we have seen none, as far as I know, and that is on 65 openings. There have been many more openings and there may have been the odd conviction, but we do not know. However, does that justify this piece of legisla-

March 14, 1978

tion which will mean that a wide cross section of people will have their mail opened? I think not.
We are entering a dangerous period in our history. If we had any reservations about whether the Solicitor General should have discretion under the Official Secrets Act, and how the Solicitor General and the government should act, surely these reservations were resolved by the evidence before the Keable Inquiry.
The evidence before that inquiry was that on January 9, 1973 an illegal break in of the PQ was inspired, not by the RCMP, but by the Privy Council office. One Liberal government decided to attack a Liberal opposition in the province of Quebec and use the full force of the law in order to do it. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, would you trust a government or a Solicitor General like this with the discretion to determine which groups of Canadians shall be subject to having their mail opened? That is what we are being asked to do in this bill.
We have evidence that the New Democratic Party of British Columbia was placed under surveillance by an RCMP agent. I do not know whether there was any involvement of the government or the Solicitor General, and we may not know unless there is an inquiry into that. How far can we trust a government and how far can we trust a solicitor general with that lack of sensitivity about what is dissent and what is subversion? This is a government that is ready to attack any person or organization that attacks it, and to use the full force of the law in order to do so. For us in this House to sit here and reward that kind of government with this kind of legislation is unthinkable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I must thank the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) who has made a stirring plea against the bill, and the spokesman for the Progressive Conservatives who delivered a masterly speech against the bill. I do not know but I think his thoughts were stronger than his voice since he ended his comments by saying he was going to support the bill.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-26 now under consideration is aimed at giving additional powers to the Solicitor General and the police to enable them to control drug traffic and subversive activities but at the same time, Mr. Speaker, it seriously infringes on one of the last strongholds of our civil liberties, that is the secrecy of mail. Through that bill, the government wants to legalize quickly what the RCMP has been doing for more than 40 years, that is to intercept and open the mail of individuals. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a statement last month which I translated from English to French and which was reported in the February 11 issue of the Montreal Star. May I be allowed to quote his statement: Like several ministers, I was not aware that illegal activities had occurred. Now we want to make them legal. He was referring of course to mail opening.
Mr. Speaker, those stories are hard to swallow. Indeed, for more than forty years the police have been illegally opening
Criminal Code
the mail of individuals and yet government authorities have the gall to say they were not aware of that kind of crime. What is to be concluded? I leave it to every knowledgeable Canadian to draw his or her own conclusion.
I would like to point out to the House that in addition to attempting to legalize a practice which already exists, no other argument or justification has been offered to us by the government. What evidence justifies the need for such powers, even if they are subject to controls? Legislation such as Bill C-26 can easily snowball and open the door to other intrusions on our basic liberties and rights.
It is reassuring, Mr. Speaker, to see that as concerns narcotics and drugs, the legislation leaves it to the judiciary to issue warrants to intercept mail on the understanding that the RCMP must have documented proof to convince the judge of the need for such police action. However, these guarantees become void in cases where the RCMP would require a warrant urgently.
Clause 178.28(2) of this bill reads as follows:
(2) Where the judge to whom an application is made pursuant to subsection (1) is satisfied that the urgency of the situation requires that interception or seizure of matter in the course of post commence before a warrant could, with reasonable diligence, be obtained under section 178.25, he may, on such terms and conditions, if any, as he considers advisable, issue a warrant in writing for a period of up to thirty-six hours.
This clause would allow the RCMP to obtain a warrant immediately without further ado. Why such a provision? We all know that drug trafficking by mail is only done on a small scale and most often in isolated cases. The RCMP itself often mentions the example of drugs sent to convicts. It seems to me that traffickers know safer and certainly quicker means than the Canadian mails to distribute their goods, since we all know that the postal service is very slow, as can vouch the unemployed who have not received their cheques these last few weeks. Moreover, the Post Office Act and the Narcotic Control Act already contain provisions in this regard. As concerns national security and subversive activities, which are the major concerns of the government, the Solicitor General would have all the authority needed without having to resort to the judiciary. The concept of national security may well become ambiguous. The Keable and McDonald inquiries have indeed shown repeatedly that the RCMP's judgment could sometimes be rather faltering. In view of the constant refusal on the part of the Solicitor General to hand over documents to the commissions I have just mentioned, we have no access to a fair and objective review of the government's actions even if in the case of the warrants issued by the courts, the Solicitor General will have to submit a detailed report as mentioned in clause 178, paragraph 34 and that, only at the end of each year.
How shall we know if the government is not abusing all the privileges vested upon it by the act? Will an eventual weak government use it in the future to spy on honest people who have every right to the confidential character of their mail? Many people will tell you that we are one of the rare countries

March 14, 1978
Criminal Code
in the world where there mail interception has not yet been made legal. This is precisely one of the reasons why we are rather reluctant to give these powers to the government and this is why this act is no matter for rejoicing.
Not having any forceful arguments to offer this House, the government is introducing this bill as temporary. Yet, in the past, interim bills have had a distinct tendency to become permanent. This is what gives me reason to doubt that the government will repeal this act, whatever the recommendations of the McDonald Commission report may be.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to quote from an article published in the Edmonton Journal on February 13 which stated the following:
The act regarding electronic surveillance passed in 1974 limited the scope of these operations to inquiries on specific crimes. These operations were limited to a 30 day period and the individual concerned had to be notified after 90 days. Some four years later, the list of crimes was extended, electronic surveillance was authorized for periods of up to 90 days, permission was granted to delay the notification for up to three years and evidence based on illegal eavesdropping was made admissible in court. Now the government intends to extend these powers to mail opening. Can we ask ourselves how long it will take before the restrictions set on mail opening also disappear?
Already the bill we have before us even goes a bit further and gives the judge the right to extend the warrants upon request from the Solicitor General, for a period of up to three years. Mr. Speaker, when in front of such a bill the government can't manage to bring forth any convincing argument, and above all, when it does not seek alternative solutions, Canadians, through their representatives, have the right to ask for iron-clad guarantees. Yet such guarantees are virtually non-existent in Bill C-26. This bill is also untimely because the McDonald Commission is presently studying that issue and should make a report on it. This bill is also arbitrary in giving so much power to policemen and the Solicitor General without too many guarantees for individuals.
To legalize the opening of mail is to take away from the citizens of a community one of the only forms of communication that still come under the seal of confidentiality. Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this bill in its present form, mainly because it does not provide adequate guarantees. Mail being the last bastion of our privacy we are rightly entitled to ask ourselves what will be the next step.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support Bill C-26 introduced by the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), an Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability Act and the Post Office Act. I will try to do so in the simplest, most logical, passionless way because this bill is too important to be used as a political instrument. That is why I would like to deal with Bill C-26 introduced today for second reading. The purpose of this bill is to give, under certain conditions, law enforcement agencies the right to open first class mail when they have reason to believe

that this would help the authorities to prevent criminal acts or apprehend their perpetrators.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to regulate freedom without eliminating it and to help neutralize certain elements whose objective seems to be to create disorder.

I am new to the Postmaster General's portfolio, but as a former mayor of Quebec City for 12 years I am not new to what constitutes sound government in the context of law and objections by the civil liberties group notwithstanding. 1 believe that Bill C-26 is a wise and necessary bill, and it will serve the best interests of the people of Canada as a whole. Furthermore, I am convinced that the built-in safeguards contained in the bill eliminate any perceived or imagined threats to the vast majority of law-abiding citizens who use the mails.
When meeting people, 1 am often asked: Is this bill really necessary? If it becomes law, what will it accomplish? All I can say is that if the legal opening of only one letter prevents only one serious crime against the state or an individual, it will have justified its existence on the statute books. If it prevents only one person from being drawn into the clutches of those who undermine the stability of our society by the veil of trafficking in drugs that is so widespread today, it will have served its purpose.
[ Translation]
In the 12 years during which I was the mayor of Quebec City, I saw perhaps more than anyone else the dangers relating to drug trafficking, the international ramifications of which are facilitated in this country by the maritime and air routes converging particularly toward Montreal and Vancouver.

Bill C-26 is designed, among other things, to make this drug trafficking a lot less profitable, and certainly a lot more dangerous than it is now for drug peddlers. Also, with a bill directed only at those who oppose the forces of law and order in Canada, what does an honest person have to fear? To think his or her letters to friends and family will be scrutinized by the police is just nonsense.
1 should like to refer, in addition, to the illegal narcotics trade, to aeroplane highjackings, bombings, assassinations, civil insurrection, and so on. These things could happen. Let us not be too naive. Why not prevent them now? This bill might help.

One must confess, Mr. Speaker, that we in Canada have been privileged with respect to criminal acts. Perhaps because of this privileged situation some Canadians could hesitate to give their support to this legislation but one should not be naive to the point of being led to believe that subversive or revolutionary forces have never been or are not at work to undermine or overthrow the democratic system in Canada or still that some criminals are not taking advantage of the great freedoms that exist in Canada.
March 14, 1978



Think about it seriously, Mr. Speaker. Is there any law-abiding citizen of Canada who would seriously argue that these dangers should be allowed to exist on the grounds that a first class letter must, under all and any circumstances, be protected by a seal of inviolable privacy? I cannot believe so, especially if the contents were known to the police. The danger I have just mentioned could be swiftly countered.

Canada is one of the only countries in the world, if not the only one, where a person is guilty of an offence any person who-and this also applies to the highest authorities-plunders, tampers, intercepts mail. This has provided criminals, and more particularly drug traffickers, with an impenetrable screen of protection, allowing them to use the mails as a messenger service without any fear of ever being caught. In Canada, at the present time, drug trafficking is done largely through the mails. One ounce of heroin is worth $2,000 and is easily hidden in an envelope.
Is there need to list all the terrible cases of drug victims? How many lives, reputations, fortunes, families have been destroyed by the evil of drugs. Hundreds! And some people would hesitate to give the police a minimum of discretion to fight those unscrupulous drug traffickers and to protect thousands of young Canadians against the pushers who only want to make a fast buck. All you need to do is to ask a city policeman to accompany him on his rounds on a weekend. You would realize that very often, the policeman is quite powerless because of laws which, in many cases, give much more leeway to the criminal than to the peace officer. Yet some are shocked by a legislation which makes it legal, under specific and closely controlled conditions, to open mail when there are reasons to believe that someone is going to commit a criminal offence or endanger the security of the state! Unthinkable!
Granted, there have been some allegations to the effect that the RCMP, albeit with the highest of motives, has for some time opened letters either being sent or received by persons suspected of criminal or subversive activities: but as far as the public, both law abiding and criminal, has been concerned, the mail system in Canada was safe from prying eyes, is safe and will be safe.
In Canada we already have legal search and wiretapping legislation. I doubt if any reasonable person would contend that the police forces in Canada should be deprived of the right to obtain warrants to search premises where there is good reason to suspect that criminal activities are taking place, or where stolen goods, arms, or ammunition are being stored. Search warrants and legal wiretapping have thus become a perfectly acceptable arm of law enforcement in this country as far as the vast majority of Canadians are concerned.
Criminal Code

The search through a person's home or office constitutes, in the strictest sense of the word, an invasion of privacy. Electronic surveillance of telephone conversations is also an invasion of privacy. Yet these two activities are now considered by most people, and with very good reasons, as necessary means to safeguard law and order in Canada.
Why is it, therefore, that the mail of criminals or saboteurs is so sacred that it precludes any surveillance aimed at enforcing the law?

I referred earlier to the built-in safeguards of Bill C-26. I think it is a wise and necessary bill, but I wish to be perfectly clear on one important point, and that is that the bill will not permit the indiscriminate opening of first class mail. [Translation]
I mentioned a while ago the safeguards which are part and parcel of this bill: the opening of the mail will have to be authorized by a warrant from a judge. The judge will ascertain what exactly the police are looking for and why the particular piece of mail has to be opened. This is a wise and necessary bill which determines under what conditions mail may be opened. [English]
It is important to understand that mail opening will have to be authorized by a warrant from a judge, that there will have to be an inquiry to ascertain exactly what the police are looking for, what they want, and why it is necessary that the letter or letters in question should be opened.
Bill C-26 seeks to ensure that the best interests of the country can be served legally, and not under the cover of some clandestine operation. The opening of mail would be subject in principle to the same legislation as that governing wiretapping. I have heard of no abuses on that score. I expect none in the opening of mail. Anyway, it will be the responsibility of the government to ensure that there will be no abuses, although it is my opinion that the way the bill is worded, none would be possible if all its provisions are strictly adhered to.
In the case of wiretapping, the person whose phone has been tapped must be so informed within 90 days. Similar provisions are contained in the bill to legalize the opening by police of first class mail. Thus, this exercise would not be carried out under an all-embracing cloak of secrecy. Where longer term surveillance than 90 days in deemed advisable, such extension may be obtained only on the presentation to a judge of an application personally signed by the Solicitor General of Canada.

One more thing in conclusion: Bill C-26 is only temporary. It will cease to be in force one year after the tabling in the House of the final report prepared by the commissioners appointed under Part I of the Inquiries Act, better known as the McDonald Royal Commission. In the course of that year,

March 14, 1978
Criminal Code
the House may consider the possibility of maintaining, amending or replacing the legislation.
In my opinion, this legislation is necessary and important. Moreover, I believe most Canadians, if they are well informed on the matter, will themselves also find it important and necessary for the protection of their liberty against every kind of abuses. For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I hope this legislation will be adopted by all parties as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my comments on Bill C-26, I would like to take the opportunity to commend the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) on the manner in which he represented our party in opening the debate. The reason I say that is that in the period of time I have been here I have heard many fine presentations and lively debates, but this subject matter goes very deeply into the depth of the Canadian soul, and the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot achieved a fine balance in his presentation. The sincerity with which he presented the case was recognized by every member of the House, and tonight I felt honoured to be a colleague of his.
The opening of mail has been going on for some time. What we are doing in this bill is to make legal that which has been done illegally before. The atmosphere in which this bill is being debated is one of suspicion on the part of many Canadians and members of the opposition of the motives of this government. The reason I say that is that in the decade that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been leader of this government, he has acquired the reputation throughout Canada of being soft on law and order. Regardless of where I go, when I speak to colleagues of mine I find they get the same feedback, that Canadians feel the Prime Minister has been soft on those who break our laws. In fact this is a permissive society, and the Prime Minister has been in the vanguard in the creation of our permissive society. The blame for a great part of the difficulties which our society is experiencing today, the pervading cynicism and the disregard for law and order, must be placed at the doorstep of the Prime Minister. It is in that atmosphere, including the events of the last six months, that this bill is now debated.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ENERGY-SMOKE DETECTION DEVICES-EFFECT OF RADIOACTIVE MATERIAL THEREIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to raise two matters concerning smoke detectors used in homes. The first is an appeal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to remove the 5 per cent federal sales tax valued at about $1 for each detector sold. The second is to raise concerns about the adequacy of the information and warnings given to home owners with respect to detectors that use small amounts of radioactive material for their operation.
Smoke detectors should be encouraged for every home. I back the use of smoke detectors. They are not unreasonably priced. They are lifesaving devices. They give early warning of smoke or fire. Indeed, they are mandatory under the national building code for new housing, and some municipal jurisdictions are considering making them mandatory in all existing housing. I am informed that the Ontario government makes smoke detectors and fire detectors mandatory in all Ontario housing for families and senior citizens across the province. The housing minister for Ontario has reported that of 64 fires in Ontario Housing Corporation units smoke detectors gave the initial warning in 54 cases, or over 80 per cent of the situations. He estimates that they possibly saved lives in 24 fires. Hundreds of thousands of smoke detectors are now in use, and I support the initiatives which have been taken so far.
I believe the federal government should now associate itself with this means of lifesaving and property saving by withdrawing its 5 per cent federal sales tax. This is what was asked for, for example, by Mr. Norman Rockall, a public spirited resident of Scarborough, who is leading a drive to have detectors installed in all Metro homes and, indeed, across Canada. Removing the federal sales tax is something the Government of Canada can do to match the fact that new federally assisted housing units must be protected by these devices. I made this request to the Minister of Finance in a letter dated February 7. I have also asked the province of Ontario to consider removing its provincial sales tax of 7 per cent levied on the retailed price, and valued at about $2.50 or $3 for an average unit. I hope my hon. colleagues will support these endeavours.
The second matter is the question of information concerning the safety of the popular ionization type detector. This ionization type, which is one of several, uses Americium 241, a highly active radioactive material which is part of the waste product from the nuclear cycle. Americium 241 is used in quantities so small as to constitute virtually no hazard, according to the Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada, which is the regulatory body. The hazard is no greater, for example, than that associated with a television set.
My research on the subject with the Atomic Energy Control Board somewhat re-assures me that in Canada, in contrast with the situation in the United States, all purchasers must be given warning of the presence of radioactive material and that they are also given some minimum instructions for disposal of used detectors. My concern, however, is about the inadequacy

March 14, 1978

of consumer education provided in this situation, the inadequacy of the information given at the point of purchase and the inadequate instructions concerning disposal.
This is the warning I found on the inside of a model 1 recently examined, and I quote:
Caution: Radioactive material,
0.9 microcuries Americium 241. Disposal by return to supplier or as directed by the Atomic Energy Control Board, Ottawa.
A notice like this raises as many questions as answers, and I was therefore pleased that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), in response to my question in the House last week, agreed to cause a review of AECB regulations relating to smoke detectors.
Here are some of the questions I think need answering: First, why are commercial procedures dealing with the use of ionization type detectors more rigorous than in the case of homes? Why must each commercial installation be approved and the facilities licensed?
Second, now that the radiation health protection branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare no longer tests prototypes of home models pending the function being transferred to the Atomic Energy Control Board under new legislation, who is testing models for safety under all conditions?
Third, what tests have been done in Canada with the ionization models, under conditions of fire?
Fourth, what right, if any, does a supplier or retail store have to refuse to accept a detector for disposal if it is returned to the supplier for that purpose? Can the supplier charge the home owner for disposal? What instructions have suppliers been given re disposal procedures?
Fifth, what guidance does AECB, in fact, give home owners who ask for directions for disposal purposes? What is the cost, if any, for disposal through the AECB?
Sixth, where, in fact, are used smoke detectors disposed of in Canada, if and when disposal directions are followed?
Finally, why is the caution sign placed inside the detector case or housing? Should it not be a requirement that the caution be put on the outside so it can be seen at the point of purchase, thus allowing the customer to make a choice among models? Should the caution not also be placed inside-

The inspection, labelling and disposal of ionization-type smoke detectors has been reviewed with the responsible authority, the Atomic Energy Control Board, which regulates these devices under the terms of the Atomic Energy Control Act and regulations as regards prescribed substances. The purpose of the legislation and the board's work is the protection of the health and safety of the public.
The criteria with respect to the minute quantities of radioactive material included in smoke detectors manufactured or imported and sold in Canada cover normal operations as well as abnormal circumstances. A simple example of this is that, in order to minimize the chance of access to the tiny radioactive source they contain, the devices must be resistant to tampering with ordinary household tools. Perhaps that helps to answer one of the hon. member's questions.
Ionization-type smoke detectors are regulated through the AECB's radioisotope licensing process, which ensures that all criteria are met. I realize how little time I have, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps I could go on to say that with regard to labelling a radiation warning label is required to be fixed to the protective housing for the minute radioactive source within this type of smoke detector. This is to indicate to anyone who sees it that penetration of the labelled barrier would result in close proximity to radioactive material. I have been assured that there is no health hazard.
From the point of view of public health and safety there should be no concern whatsoever as there is no significant hazard from AECB approved smoke detectors. However, it may be appropriate that external labelling is worth considering from the standpoint of accurate and fair marketing practices, in the interests of informing the consumer at the point of purchase and at the time of purchase. subtopic: INDUSTRY-PLASTICS-SUGGESTION INDUSTRY BE EXEMPTED FROM TARIFF CUTS
INDUSTRY-PLASTICS-SUGGESTION INDUSTRY BE EXEMPTED FROM TARIFF CUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 8 last I asked a question of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) concerning the GATT negotiations that are currently in progress in Geneva, Switzerland. Specifically, I asked the minister if he would seek an exemption for Canada's plastics industry from the general reduction in tariffs being sought by some GATT member countries.
The minister replied that Canada hopes to deal on a sector basis with non-ferrous metals at the meetings, and he said that that might well include plastics. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the minister's answer was not good enough. Given the delicate balance in our plastics industry and the fact that time is running out on the GATT talks, we can only trust that it is not

March 14, 1978
Adjournment Debate
too late for the government to make a more positive effort in this area.
The inclusion by the minister of the words "hope" and "might" in his reply only reinforces the fears in our plastics industry that the government is not pressing their case forcefully enough in Geneva. Their fears are well founded, Mr. Speaker. If certain GATT member countries get their way and the tariffs on manufactured plastic products are removed or even reduced by as much as 25 per cent, the Canadian plastics industry will be forced out of both the international and domestic markets. Not only will they become non-competitive in the world marketplace for plastic products, but countries like the United States will be able to sell their products in Canada at a cheaper price than we would be able to produce the same articles.
It must be remembered that Canada imports more manufactured plastic products per capita than any other country in the world. We import more than the United States, which has ten times our population. We are trying to overcome that imbalance in plastics products trade, but we need more time.
When Canada first ventured into the plastics industry we had to import virtually our entire requirement for raw plastics from the United States. These raw plastics included polypropylene, polystyrene and polyethylene. When I first spoke out on this problem in December 1973, Canada produced only a fraction of our needs for these raw plastics, and we did not produce any polypropylene at all. In 1973 we imported more than 70 million pounds of that particular plastic.
Our main problem is that raw plastics are a by-product of the petrochemical industry, and we in Canada do not have a petrochemical industry of any real consequence. So we lose on two counts. We lose the jobs which would be created by such an industry, and we lose the opportunity to manufacture our own needs in raw plastics. In short, Mr. Speaker, right now our plastics industry is at the mercy of countries that do have a petrochemical industry sufficient for their own needs and are also able to export the product.
We have been caught on a third count, Mr. Speaker. When the demand for plastic products began to skyrocket a few years ago, the cost of raw plastics also experienced a rise. In 1973 the cost to our manufacturers of U.S.-produced plastics rose by as much as 40 per cent, and it has continued to rise since that time. Here again, Mr. Speaker, we are trying to offset that by expanding our petrochemical industry, but it will be several years before it will come close to meeting our demands for plastic.
To give some idea of the importance of our plastic industry, Mr. Speaker, there are over 1,400 plastics processors in Canada, with plants in 125 federal ridings, and employing over 45,000 people. Capital investment in the plastics industry in Canada is in excess of $3 billion. Three billion more dollars are being invested which will double our processing capacity and create more than 25,000 high quality jobs.

It must not be overlooked, Mr. Speaker, that many other industries hiring many thousands of people depend to some extent on the plastics industry. These jobs, both the direct employment in the plastics industry and the indirect employment in other industries, are in grave peril unless Canada can convince our GATT partners that the tariffs must remain in place for the plastics trade at least for a few more years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-PLASTICS-SUGGESTION INDUSTRY BE EXEMPTED FROM TARIFF CUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is very sensitive to the claims of the hon. member. However, certain specific details should be given with regard to the plastics industry. The plastic goods consumption in Canada covers a vast array of goods and materials, which follow fairly closely the trends registered in the United States.
Because it is not profitable to produce a large number of materials from plastics, and other products, consumption being limited, it is no wonder plastic imports can represent as much as 25 per cent of the Canadian demand. However, Canadian exports amount to about 10 per cent of the local consumption. The industry is at a disadvantage with regard to exports and the competition from imports, because there is an insufficient supply of plastics in Canada; in addition, the cost of components is high as tariffs apply to most of them; and finally, because of the limited production of each article as the demand is poor for most of those goods. Those problems could be solved largely by establishing important new plastics ring plants in Canada, by access to foreign markets, and by increased productivity through greater production.
The government is working in conjunction with the industry itself on those three points, precisely to find favourable solutions. As for the GATT negotiations, the numerous representations made by the industry and individual companies have contributed much by giving the government all the available information on the problems and the possibilities for the industry that could stem from multilateral trade negotiations.
However, it would be contrary to the public interest to divulge the details of the Canadian position at those negotiations.
